options.name: Peak
options.note: Follows every peak: fast and tight.
options.use: drums, percussion, plucked bass: anything whose hits must be caught.
options.bg: peak sensing is how fast VCA and FET compressors catch transients.

options.name: RMS
options.note: Follows the average level over about 10 ms: smoother.
options.use: vocals, bass, full mixes; it follows loudness the way the ear does.
options.bg: RMS detection became the standard of VCA bus compressors from the late 1970s.

options.name: Opto
options.note: A slower average, about 40 ms, like an optical cell.
options.use: vocals, bass guitar, strings: smooth, program-dependent levelling.
options.bg: optical cells (a lamp or LED lighting a photo-resistor) made 1960s levelling amplifiers famous.

options.name: Feedback
options.note: Listens to its own compressed output: it can never fully catch up, so it eases in and sounds smoother. Ratio tops out at 5:1.
options.use: mix bus, acoustic instruments, gentle vocal levelling.
options.bg: most vintage tube and optical compressors are feedback designs; hearing their own output gives their relaxed feel.

slots.name: Curve
slots.guide: How the gain reduction grows above the threshold.

options.name: Hard
options.note: No knee: the full ratio starts right at the threshold.
options.use: drum bus, parallel smash, peak control: obvious and punchy.
options.bg: hard knees are typical of fast VCA and FET units.

options.name: Soft
options.note: Eases in over the width set by the Knee control.
options.use: vocals and the mix bus, where the start of compression should not be heard.
options.bg: soft knees spread with the 'over-easy' VCA designs of the late 1970s.

options.name: Ratio-linked knee
options.note: The knee width follows the ratio, widest at middle ratios.
options.use: general duty when you move the ratio a lot; it stays natural at every setting.

options.name: Rising
options.note: The ratio climbs as it compresses harder.
options.use: bass and vocals that swing between soft and loud: gentle on quiet parts, firm on loud ones.
options.bg: a ratio that rises with level is a trait of many tube and optical designs.

options.name: Drive into knee
options.note: A fixed 3.5:1 with a wide 11 dB knee.
options.use: vocals and guitars for a classic levelling sound.
options.bg: a moderate fixed ratio over a wide knee is the optical levelling-amplifier recipe.

options.name: Limit
options.note: A fixed 6.5:1 limiter curve with a 7 dB knee.
options.use: vocal peaks, room mics, loud drums: limiting with a soft edge.
options.bg: fixed high ratios with a knee are typical of broadcast limiters.

options.name: Vari-mu
options.note: A gentle 2.3:1 with a short 4 dB knee, like a variable-mu tube.
options.use: mix bus and mastering glue: gentle, low-ratio compression.
options.bg: a variable-mu tube's gain falls smoothly as its bias changes, which keeps the ratio low.

slots.name: Grab
slots.guide: How it clamps down when the level jumps.

options.name: Single
options.note: One smooth attack at the Attack time.
options.use: anything; the standard attack.

options.name: Two-step
options.note: Two attack stages in a row, for a softer start.
options.use: kick and snare when the click should pass but the body be held.
options.bg: a two-stage onset imitates the softer start of optical and tube gain cells.

options.name: Instant
options.note: Much faster: about a sixth of the Attack time.
options.use: peak catching, aggressive drums, room mics.
options.bg: very fast attack is the FET compressor's signature.

options.name: Knock
options.note: Knock is the plugin's FET-style compressor voicing. This part runs its own grab and curve (Curve is set aside).
options.use: drums and bass that need bite and punch.
options.bg: measured from a classic FET compressor.

options.name: Vari-mu build
options.note: A slow build over about 90 ms, whatever the Attack control says.
options.use: mix bus and pads: transients pass, then it settles slowly.
options.bg: variable-mu tubes respond slowly by nature.

slots.name: Let go
slots.guide: How it recovers after the level drops.

options.name: Plain
options.note: One smooth release at the Release time.
options.use: anything; the standard release.

options.name: Snap
options.note: A fast release, 40 ms at most.
options.use: drum rooms and aggressive parallel compression: pumping and loudness.

options.name: Glide
options.note: Recovers at a steady rate, then eases out.
options.use: vocals and bass for an even, predictable recovery.
options.bg: a steady recovery rate is how many optical and VCA circuits let go.

options.name: Two-stage
options.note: A fast 60 ms recovery, then a slow tail that builds only while it works hard.
options.use: the mix bus and full mixes: quick after transients, slow under sustained loudness.
options.bg: a dual-time-constant ('auto') release is the classic bus-compressor trick.

options.name: Release B
options.note: Release B is the plugin's name for a release that depends on depth: it recovers more slowly than the Release time after light compression, and faster after heavy compression.
options.use: dense material and vocals; it avoids long holes after big hits.
options.bg: program-dependent release is a hallmark of optical cells.

slots.name: Colour
slots.guide: Harmonic colour added by the compressor.

options.name: Clean
options.note: No colour.
options.use: classical, acoustic and mastering work, where the dynamics should be invisible.

options.name: Triode
options.note: Even-harmonic tube warmth.
options.use: vocals, bass, keys: warmth and fullness.
options.bg: triode stages produce mostly second harmonic, the 'tube warmth' of classic preamps.

options.name: Pentode
options.note: Tube saturation that gets edgier as it is driven.
options.use: guitars, synths, drum bus: bite when pushed.
options.bg: pentode stages add more odd harmonics as they are driven.

options.name: Transformer
options.note: Saturates the lows (below about 120 Hz) more.
options.use: kick, bass, 808s: weight and thickness in the lows.
options.bg: audio transformers saturate first at low frequencies, where the core's flux is highest.

options.name: Tape
options.note: Saturates the highs (above about 3 kHz) more.
options.use: drums, mix bus, acoustic guitar: softened, glued highs.
options.bg: hit hard, magnetic tape saturates and partly erases its own high frequencies.

options.name: Dense
options.note: Thickens the peaks: gentle odd-harmonic density.
options.use: drums and loud rock: fatter peaks without obvious distortion.

options.name: FET
options.note: A touch of even harmonics, like a FET stage.
options.use: vocals and snare: subtle presence.
options.bg: FET gain stages add a little, mostly even, harmonic content.

options.name: Knock
options.note: The Knock voicing's own harmonics.
options.use: drums and bass.
options.bg: the measured harmonics of a classic FET compressor.

slots.name: Colour place
slots.guide: Where the colour sits in the chain.

options.name: After gain
options.note: Colours the compressed signal.
options.use: the classic outboard sound; the colour sits after the gain, as in most hardware.

options.name: Before detector
options.note: Colours the input, so the compressor reacts to the coloured sound.
options.use: thicker, more interactive compression; the compressor reacts to the colour, like driving a unit's input stage.

options.name: Input
options.note: Steady, set by Colour amount.
options.use: a constant flavour, whatever the music does.

options.name: Gain reduction
options.note: More colour the harder it compresses.
options.use: drums and the bus: the harder it works, the more it colours, like a tube compressor running out of headroom.

options.name: Output level
options.note: More colour on louder output.
options.use: loud sections: colour that blooms with the music.

options.name: Knee position
options.note: More colour as the signal passes through the knee.
options.use: vocals: colour appears where compression starts, and quiet parts stay clean.

comp.note: Threshold, Ratio, Knee, Attack, Release and Makeup stay on the panel. If a part sets one of them, it locks it there.. that's the part doing its job.
unused: The Knock grab brings its own curve.
The Knock colour sets its own drive.
The Knock colour sets its own drive.

slots.name: Low band
slots.guide: How the low band's shelf turns. In bell mode, Passive is a plain bell.

options.name: Plain
options.note: The shelf exactly as dialled.
options.use: you want exactly what you dial, for surgical and mastering moves.

options.name: British
options.note: British console: a softer shelf that turns about an octave from the knob.
options.use: drums, vocals, modern pop and rock: punchy and a little hyped.
options.bg: the EQ of British large-format consoles from the late 1970s and 1980s.

options.name: Passive
options.note: Passive tube program EQ: a very gentle low shelf.
options.use: kick, bass, vocals, the mix bus: huge, gentle lows.
options.bg: a 1950s passive tube program equalizer; boosting and cutting the same low band was its famous trick.

options.name: Class-A
options.note: British class-A module: a firm shelf that turns well past the knob; cuts slope gently.
options.use: vocals, guitars, drums: thick, musical shelves.
options.bg: 1970s British class-A console modules with inductor EQ.

options.name: American
options.note: American console module: a broad, smooth shelf that reaches well past the knob.
options.use: drums, guitars, bass: forward and punchy.
options.bg: American console modules known for their proportional-Q EQ.

options.name: Mastering
options.note: Passive tube mastering EQ: raise Q for a resonant shelf with a dip beside it.
options.use: mastering and the mix bus: big, smooth shelves; raise Q for the resonant bump.
options.bg: a modern passive tube mastering EQ with adjustable shelf bandwidth.

slots.name: Low-mid band
slots.guide: How wide the low-mid bell is.

options.name: Plain
options.note: The bell exactly as dialled.
options.use: you want exactly what you dial, for surgical cuts and precise boosts.

options.name: British
options.note: British console: much broader than its Q says, tighter as you boost.
options.use: snare crack, vocal presence, guitar bite: broad and forgiving.
options.bg: British large-format console mids, wider than their Q markings suggest.

options.name: Class-A
options.note: British class-A module: one broad fixed width, tighter as you boost. Q is not used.
options.use: vocals and guitars: broad, musical boosts that tighten as you push.
options.bg: 1970s British class-A console modules with a fixed-width mid.

options.name: American
options.note: American console module: proportional Q, cuts mirror boosts. Q is not used.
options.use: snare, toms, guitars: boosts that narrow as you push, so big moves stay focused.
options.bg: proportional-Q, the signature of American console EQ.

options.name: Precision
options.note: Mastering parametric: a clean bell whose width follows the Q you dial.
options.use: mastering and the mix bus: narrow, exact moves that keep the width you set.
options.bg: a 1970s American mastering parametric equalizer, measured from a sampled copy (up to 6 dB).

options.name: Passive
options.note: Passive tube mid EQ: broad boosts low down, tighter up top; the cut is deeper and narrower. Q is not used.
options.use: vocals, guitars, the mix bus: a gentle presence lift or a mud dip with tube-EQ manners.
options.bg: the 1950s passive tube mid-range equalizer that partnered the program EQ, measured from a sampled copy.

options.name: Mastering
options.note: Passive tube mastering EQ: a very broad bell that narrows as you boost; Q sets how broad.
options.use: mastering and the mix bus: wide, gentle tone moves that never sound like an EQ.
options.bg: a modern passive tube mastering EQ's mid band, measured on the unit.

slots.name: High band
slots.guide: How the high band's shelf turns. In bell mode, Passive is a plain bell.

options.name: Plain

options.use: you want exactly what you dial, for surgical and mastering moves.

options.name: British

options.use: drums, vocals, modern pop and rock: punchy and a little hyped.
options.bg: the EQ of British large-format consoles from the late 1970s and 1980s.

options.name: Passive
options.note: Passive tube program EQ: the high boost is a broad bell, not a shelf.
options.use: vocals, the mix bus: a silky top.
options.bg: a 1950s passive tube program equalizer; its high boost is a broad bell.

options.name: Class-A
options.note: British class-A module: a firm shelf that turns well past the knob; cuts slope gently.
options.use: vocals, guitars, drums: thick, musical shelves.

eq.note: Frequency, Gain, Q and the shelf switches stay on the panel. Each band takes its own part, so go wild.
